title: Controlling Order & Carryover Effects
description: Neutralize practice, fatigue, and carryover effects using complete counterbalancing, partial counterbalancing, and Latin Square matrices.

slides.title: The Achilles Heel of Within-Subjects Designs 🔄
slides.content:
# When Order Distorts Reality

In repeated measures designs, the order in which conditions are presented introduces severe threats:

* **Practice Effects**: Participants perform better on later conditions simply because they got better at the task through practice.
* **Fatigue / Boredom Effects**: Participants perform worse on later conditions because they are exhausted, eye-strained, or bored.
* **Carryover Effects**: The lingering psychological or biochemical impact of one condition bleeds into the next (e.g., caffeine consumed in Condition 1 remains active in the bloodstream during Condition 2).

If Condition A always precedes Condition B, you cannot tell whether Condition B was superior or if participants simply learned how to do the task!

quizData.question: Participants solve math puzzles under Silence first, and then under Rock Music. Their scores drop during the Rock Music condition, but post-study interviews reveal they were mentally exhausted after 90 minutes of continuous testing. What threat is this?
quizData.explanation: Mental exhaustion accumulated across sequential testing conditions that impairs later performance is a classic fatigue order effect.

slides.title: Counterbalancing Strategies 🎲
slides.content:
## Mixing Up the Presentation Order

To neutralize order effects, researchers use **counterbalancing**—presenting conditions in different sequences across participants so that order effects balance out equally:

| Counterbalancing Strategy | Mechanism | Calculation / Complexity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Complete Counterbalancing** | Every possible condition sequence is tested. Equal numbers of participants are randomly assigned to each sequence. | For *k* conditions, there are *k!* (factorial) sequences. (2 conditions = 2 orders: AB, BA. 3 conditions = 6 orders: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA). |
| **Partial Counterbalancing: Latin Square** | A formal square matrix ensuring that: (1) each condition appears at each ordinal position once, and (2) each condition precedes and follows every other condition an equal number of times. | Scales efficiently: For 4 conditions, requires only 4 orders instead of 24! |
| **Randomized Block Order** | In cognitive psychophysics with hundreds of trials, conditions are presented in randomly mixed trial blocks. | Used when participants perform hundreds of rapid stimulus trials. |

Counterbalancing does not eliminate order effects; it spreads them out evenly across all conditions.

quizData.question: An experimenter has 4 experimental conditions (A, B, C, D) in a within-subjects design. How many unique presentation orders are required for Complete Counterbalancing?
quizData.explanation: Complete counterbalancing requires k! orders. For 4 conditions: 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 unique sequence orders.

slides.title: Methodological Warning ⚠️
slides.content:
### The Fatal Flaw: Asymmetrical Carryover

Counterbalancing only works if the order effect is symmetrical (Condition A affects B by the exact same amount that B affects A). If learning in Condition A permanently alters neural pathways so Condition B can never be experienced afresh (asymmetrical carryover), counterbalancing will fail! You must switch to a between-subjects design.
